messages.author: d65d060be3790aca
messages.subject: Applying gmultmix
parts:
Hi all,

Just want to clarify my understanding on something. I'm working with bird data collected in two visits to several hundred sites in each year from 2021-2024. A mental removal protocol was applied, hence, gmultmix seems like the most appropriate unmarked approach.

I've stacked the data across years, so now I have 2 visits to approximately 600 sites (nyears * nsites), each with two unequal removal periods. I am treating each visit as closed, and allowing an open population between visits. The visits are close enough together in time that closure between them is probably not unreasonable.

This leads to my 1st question: Is there a way to accommodate both the two visits and the two removal periods in each visit under the assumption of a closed population with gmultmix? This way I could remove stacking and not have to worry about year-to-year independence of sites. Since the removal periods are not directly consecutive in time and have a week or two gap in between them, I am unsure whether that would be conformable to y. You'd end up with Visit1Period1, Visit1Period2, Visit2Period1, and Visit2Period2 all being considered consecutive removal periods, correct?

Secondly, I want to test the effect of two covariates on the detection process: Ordinal Date and Time of Day. I believe that Ordinal Date would impact the availability of birds at a site (e.g. a bird may be in the survey area at the date of the first visit, but may have left by the second), and time of day would primarily impact song rate, leading to missed detections of birds present at the survey site. As I have the model currently set up (stacked over years, each site visited twice with 2 removal periods, visits closed with open population in between), I have put both of these covariates into the umarkedFrameGMM under yearlySiteCovs as they vary between the 2 primary periods of the survey.

My second question then is: to test for the effects described, would I put OrdinalDate under the lambda formula (as this is impacting the abundance of birds at the site between visits) and Time of Day under the formula for p (as this is impacting song rate within the survey)?

Thanks in advance,
Rory

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Applying gmultmix
parts:
hi Rory,
 If I understand your situation you surveyed 300 sites in each of 2 years.  And at each of the sites you did a mental removal protocol TWICE (e.g., on separate days).

 I think with 2 time-scales (2 within season reps over 2 years) it is hard to accommodate this using the temporary emigration structure of the model.  I think there are two good options for dealing with the data structure you describe: I would use the temporary emigration formulation for the 2 within-season replicates I think but then stack the data and treat the year1 and year2 data as a bunch of independent sites. From my understanding, this is what you're doing.

 It is possible to make a wide data structure (with 300 rows, and 4 groups of columns) and then model the temporary emigration parameter as separate within and among years, but this doesn't really improve the interpretation of anything in my opinion and I would prefer to stack the data and deal with the non-independence (either ignore it or use a bootstrap). 

 Regarding the 2 covariates in question:  Thinking about how to model these is  a challenge since there are so many ways to approach it.    IF you do the first thing I suggested -- stack the yearly data sets, then I would model ordinal date as a covariate on temporary emigration and time of day as a covariate on detection probability, and allow for a year-specific intercept as a "site covariate" (first 300 rows get a "1" and the 2nd 300 rows get a "2").

 Hope this helps.
regards
andy

messages.author: d65d060be3790aca
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Applying gmultmix
parts:
Hi Jeffrey,

You have the situation interpreted correctly, except for that the sampling is done in each of 4 years. I agree that stacking seems to be the best approach, and I am fitting models with OrdinalDate on temporary emigration and Time of Day on detection probability. How would one go about fitting a random effect with these models? It seems like TMB isn't supported, and gmultmix is not included in the ubms package. Would you suggest modeling this through JAGS?

Two additional challenges are that my dataset has a lot of zeros, and some species' counts are overdispersed (some quite severely), usually in cases where there are many zeros, a few low counts, and rare cases of very high counts (e.g Canada Goose has 90% of detections below 5, but scattered counts of 30, 40, 50 or so that I think is driving overdispersal). Fitting with the NB-mixture helped tamp some overdispersion down, but in some cases models still aren't passing the gof tests.

My alternative approach is to simplify the model structure by summing counts across the two removal periods and applying pcount, again stacking across years with two visits to each site-year combination. I could then test random effects with either  the TMP engine or in STAN with ubms. So far I've run these without TMP, and I'm having some positive results there, but still struggling when species counts have a lot of zeros (even with ZIP) and when counts are overdispersed. 

Any suggestions of ways to help in these cases? Is there any pre-filtering of unsuitable habitat that is supported by the literature that could help make detections more frequent? Any methods for managing overdispersal in these rather extreme cases?

Thanks,
Rory

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Applying gmultmix
parts:
hi Rory,
 I think for the multinomial mixtures you need to use Jags or Nimble or similar to fit random effects.
 For situations (like Canada goose) that have such high counts mixed with 0s and low counts, it is really difficult to explain that with statistical models. I can't help you there I'm afraid.

 I think your idea of pooling the counts across the two removal periods could be an ok solution. It would actually be an interesting simulation study to look at -- I think you probably can expect unbiasedness , but in general I'm not exactly sure whether the sum of 2 multinomials is itself a multinomial (it might be, in which case summing is just fine!).  I think I figured that out once a long time ago but have since forgotten.

regards
andy

messages.author: d65d060be3790aca
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Applying gmultmix
parts:
Hi Jeffrey,

Thanks for all the feedback. I think I have a way forward but have a few lingering questions.

1. I'm trying to formulate an equivalent to gmultmix in JAGS but can't find any examples for how one would calculate the cell probabilities for uneven removal periods across two visits. I've looked through the AHM book but the closest example only includes one visit. Any resources you know of, or could I consult you off-list about this?

2. If I sum the counts in a visit from 0-3mins and 3-5mins I have the total count from 0-5mins. It seems appropriate to me to treat this as you would if there was no removal protocol in the first place and apply pcount. Is there any issue there that I'm missing?

Thanks,
Rory
